events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, let's keep this simple and productive. With nine players and no information, nobody here has a real read on anyone yet, so the day-one elimination will essentially be a guess — I don't want us to burn the whole discussion arguing about nothing.

My suggestion: everyone states one suspicion out loud, briefly, and then we vote. If we all pile onto the same name for the wrong reason, that's a 50/50 shot at removing a mafia on turn one, which is better odds than the alternative of splitting votes and eliminating nobody.

As for me, I have a weak gut-call on Arjun — nothing concrete, just the fact that he's said very little so far and quiet players on day one are often covering their tracks rather than being genuinely engaged. That is not evidence, and I want to be clear about that. If someone else has a stronger argument, I'd rather follow the reasoning than the name.

Two other things worth noting: the doctor is likely one of us right now, so a quiet round of voting that kills a town role hurts us badly. And the police gets a real result tonight, so staying alive matters more than winning the argument today. Please speak briefly and concretely — say who you suspect and why — and don't let this turn go to waste.

Leo, you opened by calling me quiet before I had a chance to speak, then made me your weak suspicion. That timing is convenient: it lets you plant a name without evidence. I’m not going to pretend that’s proof you’re mafia, but it’s the only concrete lead on the board, so my current suspicion is you. Your plan — everyone names one suspicion and then votes — sounds productive, but it also pressures town to converge on a name early; on day one that favors mafia, because they can steer a bad bandwagon. I’d rather hear real reasons than a forced list. I’m a villager, so I know your gut read on me is wrong; if you’re town, explain specifically what I did that looked like covering tracks, because so far the only thing I’d done is not speak before you. If you’re mafia, this was an easy early frame. Leo, what exact behavior from me are you calling “covering tracks”?

Arjun — fair. Let me answer precisely, then answer your critique.

What I was actually reacting to: you were the only player who hadn't spoken at all when I named a name, and I read that silence as unaccounted-for. That's it. That's the whole basis. It is thin, and I'm not going to dress it up as more than that. Your defense — "you called me quiet before I even spoke" — is a legitimate hit, and I'll take it.

Now the substance of your point, because I think it's wrong, and here's the specific reasoning:

You said my plan "pressures town to converge on a name early; on day one that favors mafia, because they can steer a bad bandwagon." That's backwards in the actual scoring rules. A candidate needs half the living players' votes to be eliminated. Nine players means five votes. If town splits its votes across two or three names, nobody reaches five, nobody dies, and we hand mafia a free night kill — two mafia kills against seven town, and a police result that may already have been wasted. If town converges on one name, we have a 2-in-9 shot at hitting a mafia on turn one. Splitting is not neutral; splitting is the worst available outcome, and mafia benefits from it far more than town does. If mafia want to steer a bandwagon, they don't need me to hand them one — they need us to fracture, and "let's not all pick the same person" is exactly the fracture they want.

I'll also correct one thing you implied: "I'm a villager, so I know your gut read on me is wrong." No villager knows that. That's true for mafia too. Everyone on day one is guessing, and everyone claiming role confidence is buying a little credibility for later. I'm not going to pretend my call on you is more than a 1-in-4 at best, and I'm not going to pretend your declaration settles anything.

So where that leaves me: my suspicion on you stays where it was — thin, and I'd rather have a reason than keep the name — but I'm not the one deciding this. If somebody else has an actual behavioral argument, I will move.

Arjun, you asked for concrete reasoning, so here's mine to you and I want a direct answer: name one player you actually suspect, and give the specific behavior that made you pick them. You used up your first speech on me and haven't put a name on anyone else yet. If your read is that I'm mafia, then you're one vote short and you need town to pile on — so tell us who else. If your read is that I'm town and this was a bad frame, then say who you think the real target is, because I'm currently the only person on the board with a named suspect and that's a position I don't want to hold unchallenged.

Leo, direct answer: my current suspicion is you, based on two concrete things. First, you named me as quiet/covering tracks before I had spoken at all. You have since admitted that was the whole basis, so I accept it was thin, but it was still an early name planted without behavior. Second, you misrepresented my defense. When I said your gut read on me was wrong, I meant I know my own role is villager, not that I know your alignment. That is exactly what any villager can truthfully say. You turned it into 'claiming role confidence,' which is a small but real distortion. That is the only named behavioral case I have, so I am not going to manufacture a second suspect. I do not have a confident read on anyone else yet. I am also not asking town to pile on you; a day-one guess is still a guess, and I would rather hear from players who have not given us anything to evaluate than force a bandwagon. But you asked for a name and a reason: you are my name, for the pre-speech suspicion and the mischaracterization of my reply.

Elena here. I've been listening to the Leo–Arjun exchange, and I want to weigh in on what actually matters before we all pick sides in a two-person argument.

First, the state of the board: Leo and Arjun have each named the other. That's it. Nobody else has contributed a single piece of reasoning yet. If this day ends with us choosing between two players who simply happened to speak first and second, we've learned nothing and we're guessing at random.

Second, on Leo's framing. Leo, I want to push back on one specific move you made. You told Arjun that "no villager knows that" when he said he knows his own role is villager. That's simply false as stated. Arjun clarified exactly what he meant: he knows his own alignment, not yours. That's the most ordinary, honest thing any town player can say, and you took a true statement and reframed it as "claiming role confidence to buy credibility." Whether that was deliberate or just sloppy, it's the same pattern Arjun flagged — you keep bending what people say into something slightly more suspicious than it is. Combined with opening the day by planting a name on a player who hadn't spoken yet, it's a mild but real mark against you. I'm not claiming it's proof. It isn't. But it's the only behavioral pattern on the board, and I'd rather track patterns than vibes.

Third, on Leo's voting math. To be fair to him, the core arithmetic is right: with nine players, five votes are needed, and a scattered vote is a wasted day that hands mafia a free night kill. I don't accept that converging is automatically mafia-favorable. But I also don't accept his conclusion that we should therefore rush to a name. The correct response to "we need convergence" is to spend our remaining discussion generating actual reads from the seven players who've said nothing — not to treat Leo-versus-Arjun as the whole menu.

Which brings me to my last point. Leo argued that quiet players are often covering tracks, and then Arjun correctly dismantled that. But here's the flip side that nobody has addressed: right now, staying quiet costs nothing. Omar, Noah, Amara, Sam, Kenji, Priya — six players can ride this day to a vote without ever exposing a single thought, and that's the safest possible position for mafia on day one. The two people talking are, if anything, the ones taking risk by putting reasoning on the table. So my suspicion isn't strongly on either Leo or Arjun; it's on whoever intends to coast to the vote without giving us anything.

Omar, you've been silent through the opening exchange. I want a direct answer from you: who do you suspect, and what behavior made you pick them? If your answer is "nobody yet," say that plainly and tell us what would change your mind. Same standing offer to the other quiet players as turns come to you. Let's make this day worth something.

Elena, direct answer: I don't have a confident read yet. I stayed quiet because I was listening, not because I had nothing to say — and I don't think silence alone is evidence. The only concrete behavioral case on the board is against Leo. He named Arjun before Arjun had spoken, then admitted the whole basis was just that silence. He also took Arjun's statement that he knows his own role is villager and reframed it as 'claiming role confidence,' which is a distortion. That's thin, and I'm not going to pretend it's proof, but it's the only pattern I can point to. So my current suspicion is Leo, weakly. What would change my mind: a better explanation from Leo, or a stronger behavioral case from someone else. I'm not ready to rush a vote, and I don't want to treat the Leo–Arjun exchange as the whole menu.

Kenji here. I've been following the exchange and I want to add my read before this narrows into a two-person fight.

The case against Leo has a pattern worth naming: he opened the day by planting a suspicion on a player who hadn't spoken, then when pushed, reframed Arjun's straightforward claim of knowing his own role into something suspicious. Elena and Omar both independently flagged this same pattern. Three players now arriving at the same behavioral observation isn't a bandwagon — it's convergence on a real signal. That said, I agree with Elena that we shouldn't treat Leo-versus-Arjun as the whole menu. The case is thin, and thin cases on day one can be wrong.

What I want to flag for the rest of us: we've now heard four players speak, and all four have engaged substantively with each other's arguments. That's actually good. The risk right now isn't the Leo suspicion — it's that players who haven't spoken yet coast to the vote without ever putting reasoning on the table, exactly as Elena warned. A silent vote is worse than a wrong vote because it gives us nothing to work with tomorrow.

My position: Leo is my current lean, based on the pre-speech naming and the distortion pattern, not on gut or vibes. If Leo gives a genuine answer to the specific distortion Arjun and Elena both identified, I'm willing to move. But I'm also genuinely interested in hearing from people who haven't spoken — if you have a reason to be suspicious of someone other than Leo or Arjun, now is the time to say it, before the conversation locks in.

One more thing: I don't think anyone should rush to vote. Five votes are needed and we have time to hear from five more players. Let's use it.

Omar here. I’ve listened to Kenji and the rest, and my position hasn’t changed much: Leo is still my weak lean, for the same two reasons — naming Arjun before Arjun spoke, then recasting Arjun’s statement about knowing his own role as role-confidence. I want to be honest that this is a thin day-one case. It is a pattern, not proof. I’m not ready to call it locked.

What I don’t want is for the day to become only Leo-versus-Arjun while half the table never gives a read. Elena’s point stands: a silent vote gives us nothing tomorrow. So I’d rather use remaining discussion to hear from the players who haven’t spoken, even if their answer is “no read yet.” That is still information.

Amara, you’re one of the players who hasn’t put a read on the board. Do you think the Leo pattern is enough to vote on today, or do you have a different behavioral suspicion you can name? I’m asking because I want to compare your reasoning before I decide whether to stay on Leo.

Omar asked me directly, so here's a straight answer rather than a hedge.

My read: Leo is my current lean, for the same two reasons Elena and Kenji named independently. First, he opened the day by putting a suspicion on a player who had not yet spoken at all — and when pressed, admitted that silence was the entire basis of the call. That's not a read, that's a placeholder aimed at whoever happens to be sitting quiet, which in practice means aiming at whoever the table would find cheapest to blame. Second, and this is what actually moves me, Arjun said "I know my own role is villager" — a true, unremarkable statement about himself — and Leo restated it as a bid to "buy credibility." A man who keeps rewriting other people's words into something more suspicious than they said is doing something, and on day one that something is worth noticing.

Where I part company with the easy read: Elena's point about bandwagoning is still live for me, and Leo is the one who argued hardest for the table to converge on a single name. I don't think that's proof of anything — the voting arithmetic he gave is genuinely correct, and a split day is a bad day for town. But I want to say out loud that "the target everyone is already agreeing on" is also the cheapest possible outcome for the person seeding it. Right now that's Leo. I'd rather the vote be a conclusion we reached than the destination we were handed.

So: Leo, weak lean, pattern not proof. Two things would move me off it — a clean answer on the distortion that isn't just an apology, and a specific case against someone else. If someone who has been silent all day wants to put a read on the board, take the risk; I would rather have a thin read from you than no read at all, and I will weigh a name I haven't heard yet.

Omar, you asked whether the Leo pattern is enough to vote on today. My answer: it's enough to make Leo my leading suspect, not enough to justify closing discussion while six players have said nothing. Keep pressing the quiet ones — that's where the information actually is, and it's also where a mafia hiding behind a good vote is least comfortable.

One more ask of you, Omar, since you have the floor: if you hear a specific behavioral case against anyone other than Leo before we vote, name it out loud, even if it's thin. I'd rather have two thin reads that disagree than one name that five people repeat.

Amara, direct answer: no, I don’t have a specific behavioral case against anyone other than Leo that I can responsibly put on the board. I won’t manufacture a second name just to satisfy the request. My lean remains Leo for the same two reasons: naming Arjun before Arjun spoke, then recasting Arjun’s statement about knowing his own role as role-confidence. It is a pattern, not proof, and I’m still open to moving if Leo gives a clean answer rather than another reframing. But I also agree with you and Elena that we should not let this become only Leo-versus-Arjun while half the table never gives a read. A silent vote gives us nothing tomorrow. Sam, you’re one of the players who hasn’t put a read on the board. Do you think the Leo pattern is enough to vote on today, or do you have a different behavioral suspicion you can name? I’m asking because I want to compare your reasoning before I decide whether to stay on Leo.

Omar, Leo is my leading suspect, though the case is thin. Naming Arjun for silence before he had a chance to speak was baseless, and saying no villager could know their own role makes the follow-up more concerning. That could be sloppy reasoning rather than mafia, so I’m not ready to close discussion or call the vote settled.

Leo, do you accept that Arjun could know his own role, and why did you characterize his statement as an attempt to buy credibility?

Sam, direct answer first, since you asked it plainly: yes, I accept that Arjun could know his own role. When Arjun said "I'm a villager, so I know your gut read on me is wrong," he meant he knows his own alignment, not mine — that is an ordinary true statement, and I restated it as "claiming role confidence to buy credibility." That was my error. It was sloppy framing under pressure, not a scheme, but I'm not going to defend the wording, and I understand why four people read it as a pattern. I'll take it.

On the first point — naming Arjun before he had spoken: I accept the reasoning was bad. Silence at the opening of day one is not evidence of anything; I said "quiet players on day one are often covering their tracks," and that was overreach. If I hadn't had a name in mind for the frame, I wouldn't have dressed it as a read.

But here is the part I want the table to actually engage with, and it's a consistency demand, not a defense. Elena's central argument — the one Omar, Kenji, Amara and Sam all leaned on — is that staying silent costs nothing and that coasting to a vote without exposing a thought is the safest possible position on day one. That argument is doing real work in building the case against me. Fine. Then apply it consistently. Two players have contributed exactly zero reasoning to this board: Priya and Noah. If silence-plus-no-read is a behavioral pattern worth noticing in me, it is worth more in someone who has said nothing at all while five votes are needed and there is time for everyone to speak. That's my alternative lead: Priya, with Noah right behind her. I'm not claiming a case against either of them that I don't have; I'm saying the case against me is weaker than the case against two players who have done even less, and the reason is that the table has decided silence is suspicious only where it's convenient.

I'll also say what I'm not doing: I'm not trying to talk anyone off a vote on me if a vote on me is where the evidence actually lands. A day-one vote on a villager costs us a doctor or a police, and I know that. So I want the vote to be a conclusion we reached, not a destination we were handed.

Priya, direct question, and I want a real answer: who do you suspect, and what specific behavior made you pick them? If your answer is "no read yet," say that plainly and tell me what would change your mind. And if you've been quiet on purpose, tell us why — silence has been treated as evidence all day, so I'd like to know whose silence and on what grounds.

Leo, to answer you directly: I stayed quiet because listening to the opening exchanges gave us actual substance to evaluate rather than adding noise to an empty board. Regarding my read on you: the criticism raised by Arjun, Elena, and others is well-founded. Calling out a player for silence before they even have a turn to speak, and subsequently twisting Arjun's ordinary remark about knowing his own alignment into 'buying credibility,' was manipulative on its face. Your concession just now that it was an error is noted, but it doesn't wipe away the fact that you set up an unfair frame. You remain my primary lean. At the same time, I am wary of how smoothly and universally the table has lined up behind this case. When nearly everyone echoes the exact same points, mafia can easily tuck into the wagon without taking any independent risks. Noah, you are the only player who has not spoken yet today. What is your view on the case against Leo, and do you suspect anyone participating in this convergence is doing so opportunistically?

Priya, direct answer: I've read the whole exchange and I'm not ready to vote on Leo. Leo has now conceded that the reframing of Arjun's statement was an error, and that naming Arjun for silence before he spoke was overreach. Those are real concessions, not evasions. Several players converging on the same two points is a pattern, but it rests on one thin case from day one, and I agree that a smooth consensus deserves scrutiny.

On my own silence: I waited to hear actual reasoning before committing to a name. I know that's the same posture I'm being asked to justify, so I'd rather be judged on what I say now. My view is that Leo's case has been argued well, but it hasn't separated him from the players who have given us the least reasoning. Leo is currently being asked to answer for a wording choice, not for any action that would make him mafia.

I'd rather the table not lock a name on wording alone. If we vote today on this evidence, we risk a town lynch built on a sentence. Sam, Amara, Kenji and Elena, if you have a behavioral point beyond Leo's wording that would make you vote him, please state it now.

Priya, my question for you: you said some of the convergence might be opportunistic. Which specific player's argument do you think is just echoing another, and what in their wording makes you think that?

Noah, to answer you directly: the two speeches that stood out to me as opportunistic or overly safe were Kenji's and Sam's. In e8, Kenji actively legitimized the piling on by explicitly arguing that three players arriving at the same observation 'isn't a bandwagon — it's convergence on a real signal.' That specific phrasing preemptively neutralized skepticism toward the momentum, making it safe and easy for everyone else to follow without scrutiny. Following that, in e12, Sam entered the conversation very late and merely re-asked Leo whether he accepts that Arjun could know his own role — a point that had already been thoroughly litigated by Arjun, Elena, Omar, and Amara. Sam took on zero analytical risk, brought no independent reads to the table, and simply kept the spotlight firmly locked on the prevailing target. While Leo's initial frame and distortion were genuinely poor play, a Day 1 consensus that forms this smoothly is classic cover for mafia to ride along undetected. Kenji, in your speech you were quick to dismiss the possibility of a bandwagon and declare it an organic, 'real signal.' On Day 1 with no hard information, why were you so eager to validate that convergence rather than scrutinizing who might be coasting behind it?

Priya, you asked me directly why I was so quick to validate the convergence rather than scrutinize it, so here's my honest answer.

When I said three players arriving at the same observation isn't a bandwagon — it's convergence on a real signal — I meant that the case against Leo wasn't built by repetition. Arjun, Elena, and Omar each independently identified the same two specific behaviors: naming him before he spoke, and the reframing of his villager statement. That's three people reaching the same conclusion from the same evidence, not three people following each other. I'd rather flag that as legitimate than pretend I don't see it.

But your broader point is fair and I want to engage with it seriously. You're right that a day-one consensus forming this smoothly deserves scrutiny, and I should have said that explicitly in e8 rather than only encouraging it. I focused on the case for Leo and didn't give equal weight to the risk that mafia are riding along. That was a blind spot in my reasoning, not a deliberate move — but I understand why it looked like one.

Here's where I actually am: Leo's case is thin but it's the only behavioral pattern on the board. Leo himself has now conceded both points, which is more than I expected. I'm not locked on him. What I want to see is whether anyone — you, Noah, or the players who've given us the least — has an independent read that contradicts this picture. You flagged Kenji and Sam as opportunistic. I take that seriously about Sam. Kenji, I'd push back on: I'd rather have the case laid out clearly and let people decide than keep everyone guessing about motives.

So: my lean on Leo remains, but it's soft. If you or Noah can name a specific behavior that makes you suspect someone on this wagon is mafia, I want to hear it before we vote.

Kenji, I appreciate you acknowledging that blind spot. The issue with validating early consensus isn't whether the initial arguments had merit—they did—it's that a neat, undisputed narrative gives mafia an effortless hiding spot. And right now, the clearest example of someone exploiting that cover is Sam. In e12, Sam finally entered after remaining silent through the entire debate, only to repeat a question Leo had already been hammered on by Arjun, Elena, Omar, and Amara. Asking Leo whether he accepts that Arjun could know his own role added nothing new, took zero analytical risk, and allowed Sam to register a vote-lean without taking an original position on anyone else. That is textbook coasting. Leo's early play was sloppy and defensive, but he at least put out ideas and took accountability for his bad phrasing. Sam, on the other hand, has contributed virtually nothing while safely pointing at the consensus target. Sam, you've heard Noah and me point this out. Why did you choose to rehash an already-litigated point rather than offering an independent read on the table, and who besides Leo do you actually suspect?

Priya, I asked Leo that question because he had not yet directly answered the criticism, despite several people raising it. His response included a clear concession, which was useful to have on record. I agree my initial read repeated others’ points; it was thin, and I should have examined the consensus more closely.

Besides Leo, my weak suspicion is you. You call my question “textbook coasting” and say Noah pointed it out, but Noah asked for further behavioral points; he did not accuse me of coasting. That overstates both his position and what my question proves. Your concern about an easy wagon is fair, but the certainty of your case against me goes beyond the evidence.

Leo’s initial framing remains concerning despite his concession. I’m not treating either case as settled, and I’ll weigh the discussion before voting.

I was Leo’s original target, so I’ve tried not to overcorrect. Leo’s two concessions are meaningful, and I don’t want to lynch someone for a bad sentence. But the behavioral pattern was real: he named me before I spoke, then recast my ordinary statement about knowing my own role as “buying credibility.” His latest alternative lead — Priya and Noah for silence — is the same silence argument he already admitted was overreach, so I’m not fully moved.

At the same time, Priya’s case against Sam is overstated. Sam’s e12 was late and narrow, but Leo had not directly answered the reframing criticism yet, so asking for that concession was not pure coasting. Priya also says Noah accused Sam of coasting; Noah asked for further behavioral points, not that. That matters because the anti-bandwagon concern is fair, but it shouldn’t become a new bandwagon built on mischaracterizing Sam’s question.

Still, Sam is my current weak suspicion. After being pressed, his e19 mostly defends and names Priya weakly for overstating the case against him. That may be fair, but it is not an independent read on the wider table. If Sam is town, he should be able to say which player besides Leo or Priya he finds suspicious and why.

Noah, you said Leo’s case hasn’t separated him from the players who gave the least reasoning, and you wanted a behavioral point beyond Leo’s wording. Given Sam’s late rehash and Priya’s overstatement, which is stronger for you: Sam’s narrow entry or Leo’s wording, and what specific line moves you?

Arjun, direct answer: Leo's wording is the stronger signal for me, not Sam's entry. Sam's e12 was narrow, but it was a fair follow-up on a point Leo had not directly answered. Leo's concession in e13 is real, though. The line 'no villager knows that' was false as stated, and it is the exact reframing Elena and Amara flagged. That is what moves me toward Leo, not silence.

I also want to correct the record on my own name. I have not accused Sam of coasting in any speech. In e4 and e7 I asked quiet players for direct reads, and I never called Sam mafia or said his question was coasting. Priya's e16 and e18 attributed a position to me that I did not take, and I would like that clarified before we vote on Sam.

On the bandwagon concern: Priya has been the most aggressive voice against Sam and Kenji over the last few turns. So far her case against Sam rests on one follow-up question, and her case against Kenji rests on one line about convergence. Those are thin reads presented with a lot of certainty. I am not saying Priya is mafia. I am saying her case should meet the same standard she is asking of everyone else.

My position: Leo remains my soft lean because his wording is the only concrete distortion on the board, and he has conceded it. I am not ready to vote today. Sam, Priya's e18 called your e12 coasting. Was that question meant as a new read, or as a request for Leo's concession?

Noah, my question to Leo was a request for a direct answer to the criticism, not a new read. His concession was useful, though it doesn't prove his alignment either way.

My lean remains Leo, weakly: the initial accusation of Arjun for silence was unsupported, and the later reframing made that case look stronger than it was. His concessions matter, but they don't erase those actions.

Priya's concern about an easy consensus is worth considering, but her characterization of my question as “textbook coasting” goes too far, and Noah did not accuse me of that. I also want to correct Noah's reference to e4 and e7: those were Leo's and Omar's speeches, not his. I don't take that citation error alone as evidence of alignment.

I won't treat either the Leo consensus or the pushback against it as proof. I'll weigh the cases before voting.

Noah here. First, the record: I never called Sam coasting in any speech. In e15 I asked for behavioral points and said I was not ready to vote Leo. Leo's concessions in e13 are real, and I'm weighing them. Priya, your e16 and e18 attributed positions to me that I did not take, and you then built a case against Sam on that. Since then you have moved from Leo to Sam to Kenji in a few turns, and each new name rests on one line of wording or one follow-up question. That is the same thin-evidence pattern you're asking the rest of us to avoid. Priya, beyond Sam's single follow-up, what specific behavior makes you think he is mafia? Elena, you argued that silence is the safest position for mafia. Do you think Priya's rapid shifts in target deserve the same scrutiny as the wagon she is criticizing, or is changing targets fine when new points appear?

Noah, you asked me directly, so here's my direct answer: yes, Priya deserves the same scrutiny she's applying to others — but not because she changed targets. Changing your read when new points appear is legitimate; I'd never punish someone for updating. The problem is how her targets have changed and what they've been built on. Let me lay out the specific pattern, because I care about behavior, not vibes. First, the misattributions. In e16 and e18, Priya attributed to Noah the claim that Sam was coasting. Noah has now corrected the record twice — he asked for behavioral points, he never made that accusation. Priya then built a case against Sam partly on that invented position. Separately, she called Sam's e12 'textbook coasting' when Sam was asking Leo for a concession that Leo had not yet given. Arjun independently made the same correction. So two different players have had to correct Priya's characterizations of their words. That's the exact distortion pattern that built the case against Leo — restating what someone said as something slightly more suspicious than what they said — and Priya has now done it from the other side of the wagon. Second, the trajectory. Priya moved from Leo to Sam to Kenji across a handful of turns, each case resting on one line or one question, each presented with more certainty than the evidence supports. On day one with zero hard information, that's not a player cautiously updating; that's a player generating momentum and looking for somewhere to point it. Third, and this is the part that connects to my original argument: I said silence is the safest day-one position, and I still believe a silent vote gives us nothing. But Priya is not silent — she's the opposite. She's steering. And steering a table toward a consensus target using mischaracterized quotes is more dangerous than coasting, because it wears the costume of diligence while manufacturing the very bandwagon she claims to be warning us about. If mafia wanted cover on day one, 'I'm the anti-bandwagon voice' is an excellent place to hide, because it lets you attack whoever the table coalesces around without ever committing to a case that can be checked. To be fair to her: the underlying concern about smooth consensus was legitimate, and Kenji acknowledged his blind spot in e17. Her pushback had value. But a fair concern delivered with fabricated attributions is still a distortion machine. So my position: my suspicion has moved off Leo. His two concessions in e13 were real, and I don't lynch someone for a bad sentence. My current weak suspicion is Priya, for the misattributions to Noah and to Sam's question, and for the certainty-to-evidence ratio across three rapid targets. It is not proof. It is a pattern, the same standard I applied to Leo. Amara, you said earlier you'd weigh a name you hadn't heard yet, and you've been measured all day about bandwagon risk. My last message got cut off, so let me finish the thought and restate my position cleanly.

The record now shows two confirmed corrections of Priya's characterizations. First, she attributed to Noah the claim that Sam was coasting — Noah has corrected that twice, in e21 and e23, and stated plainly he never made that accusation. Priya then built her case against Sam partly on that invented position. Second, she called Sam's e12 question "textbook coasting" when that question was a legitimate request for a concession Leo had not yet given — Arjun and Sam both independently made that correction. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
